pages.heading: Guests want to redeem. They just don’t know how.
lines: Many guests add a loyalty offer and never use it in the restaurant. They don’t doubt the deal. Something breaks in the last few steps, and I was asked to find out what.
**Client:** Restaurant Brands International (RBI) – Burger King (CH, DE, UK, NZ)
**My Role:** Senior Product Designer
**Other participants:** Valentina Lopes (Product Manager)
**Platform:** BK Mobile App + Kiosk + Drive Thru
**Timeline:** Q4 2024

pages.heading: The problem: offers added, offers not redeemed
lines: Burger King’s loyalty app runs in Switzerland, Germany, the UK and New Zealand, and guests can redeem at the kiosk, the counter or the drive-thru. After in-store loyalty launched, markets reported friction: many guests added an offer, but far fewer completed the redemption.
The data showed where guests dropped off. It couldn’t tell us why.
My goal, with Valentina Lopes, our PM, was to understand what gets in the way and design a more consistent redemption experience.

chart.title: Guests set out to order on mobile, then ended up redeeming in the restaurant

groups.title: Tapped “Mobile Order” on an offer or reward
groups.subtitle: …and then completed an in-restaurant order

groups.title: Picked a service mode and restaurant
groups.subtitle: …and then completed an in-restaurant order

pages.heading: The approach: go where it happens
lines: We started at the desk with app reviews, funnel analysis, past research and competitor benchmarks. Then we went to the restaurants.
- **Field observations:** four restaurants (CH and DE), across kiosk, drive-thru and cashier ordering.
- **Interviews:** 23 guests and 3 cashiers.
- **Surveys:** post-visit, on guest expectations and scanning behavior.

pages.heading: In the restaurant
lines: Guests struggled to get their phones to connect to the kiosk. They looked around the app for their loyalty code, and some didn’t understand why a code was needed at all.
At the counter, cashiers kept stepping in to fix things by hand.
Everything we heard and saw came down to three problems.

items.title: Guests couldn’t find their code.
items.body: It lived in a tab or behind a floating button.

items.title: Pre-selection confused them.
items.body: Many didn’t know they could pre-select several offers, and some thought adding a second coupon cancelled the first because the code changed.

items.title: Buttons and language weren’t clear.
items.body: “Add to Mobile Order” and “Redeem in Restaurant” looked too similar, and the instructions sounded written for the company, not the guest.

pages.heading: Three bets
lines: Each problem became a test, with a goal of improving redemptions by more than 5%, based on funnel data from DE, CH, UK and NZ.
We could control which variant each restaurant got, so we removed the default and ran the variants against each other.

variants.label: A · Floating button
variants.note: A floating QR button over the app, opening “Your Code”: the code, with the in-restaurant order below it.

variants.label: B · Top bar
variants.note: A QR icon in the top navigation bar, opening a sheet with the code. It performed better.

pages.heading: Bet 2: Improve pre-selection or remove it?
lines: **Experiment 2** kept pre-selection and added clear feedback when guests select several offers: confirmation states and a simpler summary. **Experiment 2.2** removed it, with one offer per scan and no pre-selected cart. Both also made the loyalty code easier to find.
The results were not conclusive: neither version clearly beat the other. Both improved on what we had, but the gap between them wasn’t big enough to call a winner.

variants.label: Experiment 2 · Improve it
variants.note: Pre-selection stays, with clear feedback: a count on Scan, and a simple summary before guests scan and redeem.

variants.label: Experiment 2.2 · Remove it
variants.note: No pre-selected cart: one offer per scan, straight to the code.

compare.title: Clearer buttons
compare.description: We tested five label variations to tell “Add to Mobile Order” apart from “Use in Restaurant”, and refined the button hierarchy and icons on the offers and rewards pages.

variants.label: Control
variants.note: “Mobile Order” and “Redeem In-Store”: two actions that looked too alike.

variants.label: Winning variant
variants.note: “Scan In Restaurant” and “Add to Mobile Order”, each with its own icon.

items.label: lift in conversion, from offer added to redeemed
staff interventions, as guests could finish the journey on their own

showcase.title: The final result
intro: The top navigation bar kept performing better than the other versions, so the team shipped it and refined the UI around it: a clearer My Code page, and the new buttons from Bet 3.
It rolled out across all markets and is now part of the Guest UI/UX Standards used across RBI’s brands.
